catalog_citation: Tosco, Mauro. 2001. The Dhaasanac Language: Grammar, Texts, Vocabulary of a Cushitic Language of Ethiopia. (Kuschitische Sprachstudien 17.) Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
catalog_locator: p. 11, §1.2.2 'Grammatical profile' (publisher's free sample PDF and both confirm p. 11). Placement statements: §2.2 'Accent and tone' pp. 34-41 (per the TOC: §2.2.1 p. 36, §2.2.2 p. 37, §2.2.3 'Accent placement' p. 38) and §2.3.7 'Intonation and stress' pp. 55-60, reached only as Google Books (volume BlRpAAAAMAAJ); König 2008 and Hieda et al. 2011 cite the 'unaccented words' passage as Tosco 2001: 38-39.

new_statements.quote: At the suprasegmental level, Dh. is a fairly "classical" pitch-accent language of East Africa — but note that many monosyllables contrast for the presence/absence of accent, and that absence of accent seems on the whole far more common that its presence.
new_statements.citation: Tosco, Mauro. 2001. The Dhaasanac Language: Grammar, Texts, Vocabulary of a Cushitic Language of Ethiopia. (Kuschitische Sprachstudien 17.) Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
new_statements.locator: p. 11, §1.2.2 'Grammatical profile' (publisher sample PDF page 25; verified against page scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (29-page Köppe publisher sample). extracted text of PDF page 25 and a rendered page scan (110 dpi) both show printed p. 11, §1.2.2 'Grammatical profile', with the sentence exactly as quoted: 'At the suprasegmental level, Dh. is a fairly "classical" pitch accent language of East Africa — but note that many monosyllables contrast for the presence/absence of accent, and that absence of accent seems on the whole far more common that its presence.' (print typo 'that' for 'than' is real; the only glyph difference is the book's dash rendering in 'pitch–accent'). Surrounding section: it is the author's typological summary of the phonology; the TOC (sample p. v) confirms §2.2 Accent and tone…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dhaasanac is described as a pitch accent language: a word carries at most one (high-pitch) accent whose presence or absence is lexically distinctive (minimal pairs even among monosyllables), and most words are unaccented. The book's TOC has a dedicated §2.2.3 'Accent placement' (pp. 38-42) and §2.3.7 'Intonation and stress' (pp. 55-60), so a placement rule exists in the full grammar, but those pages are not in the open sample; the accessible statement establishes the system type, not the position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the accessible pages.
new_statements.exceptions: Many monosyllables contrast for presence vs absence of accent; absence of accent is the more common case. Mous (2012: §4.2; 2022) reports from Tosco 2001: 36 that the tone-bearing unit is the mora.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical accent (grammatical-profile statement); the grammar separately treats 'Intonation and stress' at §2.3.7, implying 'stress' is distinguished from the lexical pitch accent, but that section was not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Tosco 2001 describes Dhaasanac as spoken by the Dhaasanac of the Omo delta, SW Ethiopia (fieldwork 1998, main informant Moses Nanok Yierg'alle); Sasse 1974/1976 call the same language Galab/Dasenech and note undelimited internal dialect variation. All map to daas1238 (no separate dialect glottocodes involved).

tone_statements.quote: In particular, pitch and intensity accent with rising intonation on negative verbs emphatically affirms the positive counterpart. Uppercase characters indicate the presence of an H* pitch accent (high tone realized on the stressed syllable) on a syllable. … Diacritics represent tones. … Dhaasanac is a tone language as the following minimal tonal pairs suggest: (4) a. ár “bull” - ar “song” b. éllu “back” - ellu “cheeks”
tone_statements.locator: p. 245 (text before ex. 3 and fn. 21) and p. 246 (ex. 4), section 'Focus Equivalent To Another Negation'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Calls Dhaasanac a tone language, citing two minimal tonal pairs (ár 'bull' vs ar 'song', éllu 'back' vs ellu 'cheeks'); no tone inventory given; corrective focus is an H* pitch accent plus stress.

sources.note: From Google Books snippets: verb paradigms are characterised by a 'prosodic morpheme' (sec. 1.2 'Prosodic Morpheme of Dasenach Verbs and Allomorphs'); the Imperfect template is bimoraic stem + -a, the Imperative template is 'H CV(V)C', i.e. a High tone is part of the morphological template, with a remark on 'tone in the penultimate mora'. So the paper treats high tone/accent as a grammatical (templatic) exponent in verb inflection - grammatical-tone evidence complementary to Tosco 2001's accent chapter; not a full tonology.
